text: Graphic design. Graphic design combines graphical elements and design principles to communicate a message to an audience.
Line. A line is a visible path. It can divide, connect, outline, or guide.
Color. Color is a visual quality we can change to identify, group, emphasise, or suggest a mood.
Shape. A shape is a two-dimensional area with a boundary.
Texture. Texture is the appearance or feel of a surface. A flat image can suggest a texture.
Space. Space includes the areas occupied by elements and the empty areas within, around, or between them.
Form. Form concerns three-dimensional volume. A flat image can suggest form through light, shadow, and perspective.
Typography. Typography is the visual presentation of written language: letterforms, size, weight, spacing, and arrangement.
Contrast. Contrast is a visible difference between elements, such as light and dark, big and small, or straight and curved.
Hierarchy. Hierarchy establishes an order of importance so viewers know what to notice first and next.
Alignment. Alignment places elements along shared edges, centres, or guides.
Balance. Balance distributes visual weight. It can be symmetrical or asymmetrical.
Proximity. Proximity places related elements close together so their relationship is clearer.
Repetition. Repetition reuses selected visual features to create consistency.
Simplicity. Simplicity removes unnecessary complication while keeping what the message needs.
Function. Function asks whether the design helps its intended audience understand or do what the brief requires.
